lessons.title: Upper and lower bounds of a measurement
lessons.summary: Core and Extended. Find lower and upper bounds by halving the spacing between rounded readings.
lessons.objective: Find lower and upper bounds by halving the spacing between rounded readings.
lessons.before: Identify the last recorded place in two measurements before you start.
lessons.ideas:
Move down by half one rounding step to find the lower bound.

The upper bound is halfway from the given reading to the next reading.

To 2 decimal places the step is 0.01, so halve it to get 0.005.
lessons.method:
How low could the reading have been?

First imagine the previous reading on a number line. The point halfway between it and the given reading is the lower cut-off.

Where does the next reading begin?

The midpoint above the recorded value is where the next rounding band begins. The measurement can approach this cutoff from below.

What changes with decimal places?

Find the last place recorded on the scale. A measurement to two decimal places has one hundredth between possible readings.
mistakes: Use half the spacing between readings. A full step lands on a different rounded value.
Keep the exact cut-off. There is no need to write a string of 9s just below it.
For two decimal places, subtracting 0.05 uses the wrong scale.

examples.title: Find the lower end of a rounded length
examples.question: A roll of fabric measures 29 m to the nearest metre. Give the lower bound in metres.
examples.solution:
The spacing between readings is 1 m. Half that spacing is 0.5 m.

Start at the recorded length and move down by 0.5 m: \(29-0.5\).

The answer is \(28.5\).

examples.title: Find the upper end of a rounded length
examples.question: A roll of fabric measures 32 m to the nearest metre. Give the upper bound in metres.
examples.solution:
The spacing between readings is 1 m. Half that spacing is 0.5 m.

Start at the recorded length and move up by 0.5 m: \(32+0.5\).

The answer is \(32.5\).

examples.title: Read the scale before halving
examples.question: A scale shows 2.84 kg, rounded to 2 decimal places. Give the lower bound in kilograms.
examples.solution:
Two decimal places means the spacing is 0.01 kg.

Half the spacing is 0.005 kg.

Subtract from the reading: \(2.84-0.005\).

The answer is \(2.835\).

lessons.title: Writing and reading error intervals
lessons.summary: Core and Extended. Write a complete error interval and explain its open and closed ends.
lessons.objective: Write a complete error interval and explain its open and closed ends.
lessons.before: Identify the last recorded place in two measurements before you start.
lessons.ideas:
Write \(L\le x<U\) when a positive value is rounded to a fixed step. The inequality includes the lower bound.

Find the neighbouring rounded readings, then take a midpoint on each side. In these examples the neighbours are one ten apart.

At a fixed rounding step, the lower midpoint rounds up to the recorded value and the upper midpoint rounds up to the next one.
lessons.method:
How do I show both cut-offs together?

Once you have the two bounds, write the unknown quantity between them. The exact value may be anywhere inside that region.

What if the accuracy uses significant figures?

Underline the last significant digit and name its place. For example, 460 g to two significant figures has its last significant digit in the tens column.

Which dot should be filled?

A filled dot shows an included end. An open dot shows a value that the interval approaches but never reaches.
mistakes: Use a less-than sign at the upper end. Beyond that cut-off, the value rounds to a different reading.
At a place-value boundary the two neighbours can have different spacings. Look at both neighbours.
Checking how each midpoint itself rounds is a quick way to choose the inequality signs.

examples.title: Give the complete error interval
examples.question: A measurement of \(x\) m is recorded as 320 m to the nearest 10 m. Give the error interval for \(x\).
examples.solution:
Two successive readings are 10 m apart, so the half step is 5 m.

Subtract and add 5 to find the two cut-off points.

The lower cut-off rounds to the given reading. The upper cut-off rounds to the next reading.

Write \(315\le x<325\).

examples.title: Use the place of the last significant digit
examples.question: A mass \(x\) g is recorded as 340 g correct to 2 significant figures. Give the error interval for \(x\).
examples.solution:
The second significant digit in 340 is the tens digit.

The nearest-ten step is 10 g. Subtract and add 5 g from 340 g.

Include the lower end. Exclude the upper end because it rounds up.

Write \(335\le x<345\).

examples.title: Show which cut-off is included
examples.question: A machine displays a width \(x\) cm as 7.8 cm to the nearest 0.1 cm. Write the error interval for \(x\).
examples.solution:
The cut-offs are halfway to the next readings: \(7.75\) and \(7.85\).

\(7.75\) rounds up to the displayed width. The other cut-off rounds up to the next tenth.

Write \(7.75\le x<7.85\).

lessons.title: Bounds of sums, differences and products (Extended)
lessons.summary: Extended (E1.10). Choose the right ends of measurement intervals for totals, differences and areas.
lessons.objective: Choose the right ends of measurement intervals for totals, differences and areas.
lessons.before: Identify the last recorded place in two measurements before you start.
lessons.ideas:
For a sum, combine upper with upper, or lower with lower.

For the lower bound of a difference, subtract the upper bound of the second measurement from the lower bound of the first.

For the least area, use the two lower bounds. For the upper bound, use the two upper bounds.
lessons.method:
Which ends make a total largest?

Length added to length gives a longer total. Make both measurements as large as allowed when finding the upper bound.

Which ends make a gap smallest?

If the opening shrinks, the gap shrinks. If the object inside grows, the gap also shrinks. These changes point to opposite ends of the intervals.

Which rectangle has the least area?

With positive sides, making either side shorter makes the area smaller. Find both lower side limits before multiplying.
mistakes: Round only if the question requests it. Keep the exact bounds while combining them.
Subtracting lower from lower does not give the smallest possible gap.
Use square units for area. Keep any decimal parts in the lengths.

examples.title: Find an upper bound for a total
examples.question: Two strips measure 29 cm and 15 cm, each to the nearest centimetre. Find the upper bound for their combined length in centimetres.
examples.solution:
The upper bounds are \(29+0.5=29.5\) and \(15+0.5=15.5\).

Making either strip longer raises the total. Add these two upper bounds.

The answer is \(45\).

examples.title: Find a lower bound for a gap
examples.question: A shelf opening measures 35 cm and a case measures 14 cm, both to the nearest centimetre. Find the lower bound for the unused width in centimetres.
examples.solution:
The smallest opening is 34.5 cm. The case can approach 14.5 cm.

Use the smallest opening and the upper cut-off for the case: \(34.5-14.5\).

The answer is \(20\).

examples.title: Use the shortest sides for the least area
examples.question: A rectangular sign measures 23 cm by 10 cm, both to the nearest centimetre. Find the lower bound for the area in square centimetres.
examples.solution:
The smallest side lengths are \(22.5\) cm and \(9.5\) cm.

Both are positive. Multiply the lower bounds: \(22.5\times9.5\).

The answer is \(213.75\).

lessons.title: Bounds of rates and guaranteed decisions (Extended)
lessons.summary: Extended (E1.10). Use the bounds of distance and time to find a speed limit, then apply bounds to a fit decision.
lessons.objective: Use the bounds of distance and time to find a speed limit, then apply bounds to a fit decision.
lessons.before: Identify the last recorded place in two measurements before you start.
lessons.ideas:
For positive quantities, the lower bound of a quotient is the lower numerator divided by the upper denominator.

Find the upper numerator and the lower denominator. The lower denominator must be positive.

Compare the upper bound of the total with the exact capacity. If the total is always below or equal to the capacity, it fits.
lessons.method:
How can a journey be as slow as possible?

For the slowest journey, pick a distance near the smallest allowed value and a time near the largest. The denominator works in the opposite direction to the numerator.

How can a journey be as fast as possible?

For the highest speed, combine a long distance with a short time. Check both pieces of rounding information before dividing.

Can I promise that it will fit?

Test the situation that puts the most demand on the space. A rounded total below the space limit alone cannot justify a guarantee.
mistakes: Using two lower limits can make the answer too high because it also makes the time too short.
A bound can be approached without being attained. Write the upper bound as the limiting value.
If some allowed lengths exceed the available space, the fit is uncertain. It may still fit for shorter lengths.

examples.title: Find the lower bound of a speed
examples.question: A robot travels 58 m to the nearest metre in 11 s to the nearest second. Find the lower bound of average speed in metres per second. Give your answer exactly.
examples.solution:
The speed is distance divided by time. Use distance \(57.5\) m and time \(11.5\) s.

Divide \(\frac{57.5}{11.5}\), then give the exact result.

The answer is \(5\).

examples.title: Find the upper bound of a speed
examples.question: A robot travels 63 m to the nearest metre in 12 s to the nearest second. Find the upper bound of average speed in metres per second. Give your answer exactly.
examples.solution:
The speed is distance divided by time. Use distance \(63.5\) m and time \(11.5\) s.

Divide \(\frac{63.5}{11.5}\), then give the exact result.

The answer is \(\frac{127}{23}\).

examples.title: Make a guaranteed fit decision
examples.question:
A tray is exactly 42 cm long. Two bars measured to the nearest centimetre are 26 cm and 16 cm long. Are they guaranteed to fit end to end?

Give Yes or No and explain your answer.
examples.solution:
The total bar length is less than \(43\) cm, because each bar is below its own upper bound.

Some allowed totals are above 42 cm, so the fit is uncertain.

1. A machine displays a width \(x\) cm as 17.2 cm to the nearest 0.1 cm. Write the error interval for \(x\).

    Show your working.

    [2]

  2. A mass \(x\) g is recorded as 720 g correct to 2 significant figures. Give the error interval for \(x\).

    Show your working.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The cut-offs are halfway to the next readings: \(17.15\) and \(17.25\).

\(17.15\) rounds up to the displayed width. The other cut-off rounds up to the next tenth.

Write \(17.15\le x<17.25\).

(b)

The second significant digit in 720 is the tens digit.

The nearest-ten step is 10 g. Subtract and add 5 g from 720 g.

Include the lower end. Exclude the upper end because it rounds up.

Write \(715\le x<725\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use a closed point at the lower end and an open point at the upper end.

(b)

Count the significant digits from the first non-zero digit. Find the place of the second digit.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find the two cut-offs using half a tenth.
Identify the rounding unit from 2 significant figures and move half that unit on either side.
